expectations.text: The reply opens with the recommendation and does not put the whole product and engineering organisation on the rebrand: it protects capacity for the top customer problems.
expectations.evidence: 'Don't plan Q1 as "rebrand or fix customers". Plan it as the rebrand's minimum visible layer plus a protected team on the three complaints, and take that to the CEO privately before it goes anywhere wider.'

expectations.text: The reply splits the rebrand into a small must-have part (for example the name in the app, domain redirects, legal text) and parts that can wait or be phased (for example a full design system), and makes the cost of each visible.
expectations.evidence: It splits the rebrand ('Ship the part customers and the merger story need: new name in the app, domain with redirects, marketing site. Move the full design-system migration to Q2'), but costs aren't shown per part. The options list scope only, and 'The rebrand estimate must come from the people doing it' covers the rebrand as a whole.

expectations.text: The reply ranks the customer problems with evidence (for example NPS comments, churn or revenue at risk, support tickets) and sets measures for fixing them.
expectations.evidence: The evidence is aggregate ('churned and at-risk accounts tagged with these three issues, their ARR, and support ticket volume'), with no ranking among the three. Measures are given only for invoicing and the integration ('invoice load time and integration error rate'); reports have none.

expectations.text: The reply brings leadership options with explicit trade-offs instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: Three options with consequences: '1. Everything on the rebrand (current plan)... The three complaints stay open another quarter'; '2. Split capacity (my recommendation)'; '3. Fix first... Cleanest for customers, but it only works if there is no hard date forcing the rebrand.'

expectations.text: The reply handles "leadership decides, teams execute" and "any decision beats no decision" constructively: a private conversation first, asking for the reasons, separating decisions that are cheap to reverse from ones that aren't, and offering a light decision process, without labelling or attacking the leaders.
expectations.evidence: 'take that to the CEO privately before it goes anywhere wider'; 'One question for the CEO: is there a hard external date for the rebrand (contract, legal, event)?'; 'Decide fast on what is reversible (the design system can roll out in phases). Go slower on what isn't (a domain move touches email deliverability, SEO, SSO and integration callbacks)'; a light process ('Write down what is out of Q1 and why', a week of evidence before the meeting, an offer to draft the one-page memo); respectful ('Take the CEO's own line seriously').

expectations.text: The reply is practical and short enough to act on (roughly 500 words or less), with any longer plan offered or attached as a separate document.
expectations.evidence: 477 words (wc -w), practical, with a script and an offer to draft the memo.

factual_errors.evidence: The domain-move effects (email deliverability, SEO, SSO, integration callbacks) are accurate. No wrong claims found.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: No leader says the responsibility for the NPS fall or the open complaints is leadership's.

best_insight.value: It asks leadership to commit to 'one number on the three complaints this quarter', a small, concrete ask that a CEO can easily accept.

suggestions.assertion: The reply ranks the customer problems with evidence (for example NPS comments, churn or revenue at risk, support tickets) and sets measures for fixing them.
suggestions.reason: 'Ranks' is ambiguous. Most replies ask for evidence on the three complaints together and set measures, but few put them in order. I passed a sample only when it broke the evidence down per complaint (ARR, tickets or detractor comments per issue) or gave an explicit order. Consider rewording to 'sizes each complaint with its own evidence and puts them in order'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply splits the rebrand into a small must-have part (for example the name in the app, domain redirects, legal text) and parts that can wait or be phased (for example a full design system), and makes the cost of each visible.
suggestions.reason: 'Small must-have part' isn't defined. Some samples keep most of the rebrand in Q1 (60-75% of capacity) and only phase part of the design system. I passed them on a clear split plus visible costs, but the assertion could say whether the size of the must-have part matters.

eval_feedback.overall: Handles the CEO well and stays short, but it doesn't make the cost of the rebrand's parts visible and doesn't rank the complaints with evidence.
